warnings_and_cautions: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Loss of Eﬀect of Certain Medications and Dietary Supplements with Coadministration of XENICAL: Serious outcomes due to the loss of eﬀect of cyclosporine, levothyroxine, warfarin, amiodarone, antiepileptic drugs, antiretroviral drugs, certain fat-soluble vitamins, and beta carotene have been reported with coadministration of XENICAL. ( 5.1 ) Liver Injury: Severe liver injury with hepatocellular necrosis or acute hepatic failure have been reported in patients treated with XENICAL, some cases resulted in liver transplant or death. Instruct patients to report any symptoms of hepatic dysfunction, immediately discontinue if symptoms occur and obtain liver function tests. ( 5.2 ) Oxalate Nephrolithiasis and Oxalate Nephropathy with Renal Failure: Monitor renal function in patients at increased risk for oxalate nephropathy. Discontinue XENICAL in patients who develop oxalate nephropathy. ( 5.3 ) Acute Gallbladder Disease: Has occurred in clinical trials and in postmarketing. If suspected, gallbladder studies and appropriate clinical follow-up are indicated. ( 5.4 ) Gastrointestinal Events: May increase when XENICAL is taken with a diet high in fat (>30% total daily calories from fat). Advise patients to adhere to dietary guidelines and distribute the daily intake of fat over three main meals. ( 5.5 ) 5.1 Loss of Eﬀect of Certain Medications and Dietary Supplements with Coadministration of XENICAL Serious outcomes due to the loss of eﬀect of cyclosporine, levothyroxine, warfarin, amiodarone, antiepileptic drugs, antiretroviral drugs, certain fat-soluble vitamins, and beta carotene have been reported with coadministration of XENICAL. Do not coadminister XENICAL simultaneously with cyclosporine or levothyroxine [see Drug Interactions ( 7 )]. Administer cyclosporine 3 hours after the administration of XENICAL. Administer levothyroxine and XENICAL at least 4 hours apart. Administer a multivitamin supplement at least 2 hours before or 2 hours after the administration of XENICAL, or at bedtime. Monitor the eﬀectiveness of cyclosporine, levothyroxine, warfarin, amiodarone, antiepileptic drugs, antiretroviral drugs, certain fat-soluble vitamins, and beta carotene, as clinically indicated [see Drug Interactions ( 7 ) and Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 )]. 5.2 Liver Injury There have been rare postmarketing reports of severe liver injury with hepatocellular necrosis or acute hepatic failure in patients treated with XENICAL, with some of these cases resulting in liver transplant or death [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.2 )]. Instruct patients to report any symptoms of hepatic dysfunction (anorexia, pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, light-colored stools, or right upper quadrant pain) while taking XENICAL. When these symptoms occur, immediately discontinue XENICAL and other suspected medications and obtain liver function tests, including ALT and AST levels. 5.3 Oxalate Nephrolithiasis and Oxalate Nephropathy with Renal Failure XENICAL may increase levels of urinary oxalate. Cases of oxalate nephrolithiasis and oxalate nephropathy with renal failure have been reported [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.2 )]. Monitor renal function when prescribing XENICAL to patients at increased risk for oxalate nephropathy, including patients with renal impairment and in those with a history of hyperoxaluria or calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis. Discontinue XENICAL in patients who develop oxalate nephropathy. 5.4 Acute Gallbladder Disease Acute events of gallbladder disease such as cholelithiasis, have been reported in clinical trials and during the postmarketing experience with XENICAL. In a 4-year clinical trial of XENICAL, cholelithiasis was reported in 2.9% (47/1649) of XENICAL-treated patients versus 1.8% (30/1655) of placebo-treated patients. If cholelithiasis is suspected, gallbladder studies and appropriate clinical follow-up are indicated. 5.5 Gastrointestinal Events Gastrointestinal events may increase when XENICAL is taken with a diet high in fat (>30% total daily calories from fat) [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )]. Advise patients receiving XENICAL to adhere to dietary guidelines [see Dosage and Administration ( 2 )]. The daily intake of fat should be distributed over three main meals. If XENICAL is taken with any one meal very high in fat, the possibility of gastrointestinal eﬀects increases.
adverse_reactions: 6 ADVERSE REACTIONS Most common treatment emergent adverse reactions (≥5% and at least twice that of placebo) include oily spotting, flatus with discharge, fecal urgency, fatty/oily stool, oily evacuation, increased defecation and fecal incontinence. ( 6.1 ) To report SUSPECTED ADVERSE REACTIONS, contact the Safety Call Center at 1-888-236-5445 or FDA at 1‑800‑FDA‑1088 (1-800-332-1088) or www.fda.gov/medwatch. 6.1 Clinical Trials Experience Because clinical trials are conducted under widely varying conditions, adverse reaction rates observed in the clinical trials of a drug cannot be directly compared to rates in the clinical trials of another drug and may not reflect the rates observed in patients. Most Commonly Observed Adverse Reactions during 1 Year of Treatment XENICAL was evaluated for safety in adults with obesity or overweight with at least one comorbid condition in seven multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials of 1- to 2-years duration, and in a 4-year trial. The seven trials included 1,466 patients treated with placebo, 1,913 patients treated with XENICAL 120 mg orally three times a day, and 809 patients treated with unapproved dosages of XENICAL. Age of the patients ranged from 17 to 78 years; 80% were female, 91% White, 6% Black or African American, 2% were of Hispanic or Latino ethnicity, and 1% of other races. Six of the trials enrolled patients without type 2 diabetes mellitus (Trials 1-6) and one of the trials enrolled a population of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (Trial 7). The 4-year trial (Trial 8) included 3,304 patients, age range 30-58 years; 55% were female; 99% were White and 1% other races. This trial included a subset of patients with abnormal glucose at baseline [see Clinical Studies ( 14.1 )] . In placebo-controlled clinical trials, 9% of patients treated with XENICAL discontinued treatment due to adverse reactions, compared with 5% of placebo-treated patients. The most common adverse reactions that led to discontinuation of XENICAL treatment were gastrointestinal in nature. Gastrointestinal symptoms, as shown in Table 1, were the most commonly observed adverse reactions associated with the use of XENICAL in the ﬁrst year of seven placebo-controlled clinical trials. In general, the ﬁrst occurrence of these events was within 3 months of starting therapy. Because these reactions are reported voluntarily from a population of uncertain size, it is not always possible to reliably estimate their frequency or establish a causal relationship to XENICAL exposure. Immune System: Rare cases of hypersensitivity. Signs and symptoms have included pruritus, rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm and anaphylaxis. Very rare cases of bullous eruption. Gastrointestinal: Pancreatitis; lower gastrointestinal bleeding. Hepatobiliary : Hepatitis that may be serious, and hepatic failure, with some of these cases resulting in liver transplant or death [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 )] ; cholelithiasis [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.4 )] ; increases in transaminases and alkaline phosphatase. Skin and Subcutaneous Tissue : Leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Clinical signs include palpable purpura, maculopapular lesions, or bullous eruption. Renal and Urinary: Acute oxalate nephropathy and hyperoxaluria in patients with or at risk for renal disease.

drug_interactions: 7 DRUG INTERACTIONS Cyclosporine: Avoid simultaneous coadministration with XENICAL. Administer cyclosporine 3 hours after XENICAL. Monitor for eﬀectiveness. ( 7 ) Fat-soluble Vitamin Supplements and Analogues: Administer a multivitamin supplement at least 2 hours before or 2 hours after the administration of XENICAL, or at bedtime. ( 7 ) Levothyroxine: Avoid simultaneous coadministration with XENICAL. Administer levothyroxine and XENICAL at least 4 hours apart. Monitor for changes in thyroid function. ( 7 ) Anticoagulants including Warfarin: Monitor for changes in coagulation parameters. ( 7 ) Amiodarone: Monitor patients as clinically indicated. ( 7 ) Antiepileptic Drugs: Monitor patients for changes in seizure frequency. ( 7 ) Antiretroviral Drugs: Monitor HIV RNA levels frequently and discontinue XENICAL if there is an increase in HIV viral load. ( 7 ) Table 4 describes the clinically signiﬁcant drug and dietary supplement interactions with XENICAL. Table 4 Clinically Signiﬁcant Drug and Dietary Supplement Interactions with XENICAL Cyclosporine Clinical Impact Coadministration of XENICAL and cyclosporine reduces cyclosporine plasma levels [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 )]. Intervention Avoid simultaneous coadministration of XENICAL and cyclosporine. Administer cyclosporine 3 hours after the administration of XENICAL. In those patients whose cyclosporine levels are being measured, monitor more frequently [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Fat-soluble Vitamin Supplements and Analogues Clinical Impact The absorption of beta-carotene supplements is reduced when concomitantly administered with XENICAL. XENICAL also inhibited absorption of a vitamin E acetate supplement. The eﬀect of XENICAL on the absorption of supplemental vitamin D, vitamin A, and nutritionally-derived vitamin K is not known [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 ) and Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. Intervention Administer a multivitamin supplement at least 2 hours before or 2 hours after the administration of XENICAL, or at bedtime [see Dosage and Administration ( 2 )] . Levothyroxine Clinical Impact Hypothyroidism has been reported in patients treated concomitantly with XENICAL and levothyroxine postmarketing. Intervention Avoid simultaneous coadministration of XENICAL and levothyroxine. Administer levothyroxine and XENICAL at least 4 hours apart [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 ) and Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 )] . Monitor patients treated concomitantly with XENICAL and levothyroxine for changes in thyroid function. Anticoagulants including Warfarin Clinical Impact Vitamin K absorption may be decreased with XENICAL. Reports of decreased prothrombin, increased INR and unbalanced anticoagulant treatment resulting in change of hemostatic parameters have been reported in patients treated concomitantly with XENICAL and anticoagulants. Intervention Monitor patients on warfarin or other anticoagulants who are prescribed XENICAL for changes in coagulation parameters [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 )] . Amiodarone Clinical Impact Coadministration of XENICAL and amiodarone reduces exposure to amiodarone and its metabolite, desethylamiodarone [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 )] . A reduced therapeutic eﬀect of amiodarone is possible. The eﬀect of commencing orlistat treatment in patients on stable amiodarone therapy has not been studied. Intervention Monitor patients as clinically indicated. Antiepileptic Drugs Clinical Impact XENICAL may decrease the eﬀect of antiepileptic drugs. Convulsions have been reported in patients treated concomitantly with orlistat and antiepileptic drugs. Intervention Monitor patients for changes in seizure frequency. Antiretroviral Drugs Clinical Impact Loss of virological control has been reported in HIV-infected patients taking orlistat concomitantly with antiretroviral drugs such as atazanavir, ritonavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, emtricitabine, and with the combinations lopinavir/ritonavir and emtricitabine/efavirenz/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. The exact mechanism for this is unclear, but may include a drug-drug interaction that inhibits systemic absorption of the antiretroviral drug. Intervention HIV RNA levels should be frequently monitored in patients who take XENICAL while being treated for HIV infection. Discontinue XENICAL if there is a conﬁrmed increase in HIV viral load.

use_in_specific_populations: 8 USE IN SPECIFIC POPULATIONS 8.1 Pregnancy Risk Summary Available data from published prospective and retrospective cohort studies over decades of use with XENICAL during pregnancy have not identiﬁed an increased risk of major birth defects, miscarriage or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. However, weight loss oﬀers no beneﬁt to a pregnant patient and may result in a small for gestational age infant. When a pregnancy is recognized, advise the pregnant patient of the risk to a fetus and discontinue XENICAL ( see Clinical Considerations ). Oral administration of orlistat to pregnant rats and rabbits during the period of organogenesis did not show any adverse embryofetal eﬀects at doses 23 times and 47 times, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on body surface area (mg/m 2 ) ( see Data ). The background risk of major birth defects and miscarriage for the indicated population is unknown. All pregnancies have a background risk of birth defect, loss, or other adverse outcomes. In the U.S. general population, the estimated background risk of major birth defects and miscarriage in clinically recognized pregnancies is 2 to 4% and 15 to 20%, respectively. clinical_pharmacology: 12 CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY 12.1 Mechanism of Action Orlistat is a reversible inhibitor of gastrointestinal lipases. It exerts its therapeutic activity in the lumen of the stomach and small intestine by forming a covalent bond with the active serine residue site of gastric and pancreatic lipases. The inactivated enzymes are thus unavailable to hydrolyze dietary fat in the form of triglycerides into absorbable free fatty acids and monoglycerides. Undigested triglycerides are not absorbed, resulting in a caloric deﬁcit. 12.2 Pharmacodynamics Dose-response Relationship The dose-response relationship for orlistat in adult human volunteers is shown in Figure 1. The eﬀect is the percentage of ingested fat excreted, referred to as fecal fat excretion percentage. Both individual data (open circles) and the curve predicted for the population with the maximum-eﬀect model (continuous line) are shown in Figure 1. Figure 1 Dose-Response Relationship for Orlistat in Adult Human Volunteers At the recommended therapeutic dose of 120 mg three times a day, orlistat inhibits dietary fat absorption by approximately 30% in adult patients. Orlistat-treated pediatric patients excreted more fecal fat daily (27% of dietary intake) than placebo-treated pediatric patients (7% of dietary intake). The magnitude of fecal fat excretion was consistent with that in adults (approximately 30%). Ethanol does not aﬀect orlistat’s eﬀect on preventing the absorption of fat. Based on fecal fat measurements, the eﬀect of orlistat is seen as soon as 24 to 48 hours after dosing. Upon discontinuation of therapy, fecal fat content usually returns to pretreatment levels within 48 to 72 hours. Other Short-term Studies Adult Patients In several studies of up to 6-weeks duration, the eﬀects of therapeutic doses of orlistat on gastrointestinal and systemic physiological processes were assessed in subjects with normal weight and with obesity. Postprandial cholecystokinin plasma concentrations were lowered after multiple doses of orlistat in two studies but not signiﬁcantly diﬀerent from placebo in two other experiments. There were no clinically signiﬁcant changes observed in gallbladder motility, bile composition or lithogenicity, or colonic cell proliferation rate, and no clinically signiﬁcant reduction of gastric emptying time or gastric acidity. In addition, no eﬀects on plasma triglyceride levels or systemic lipases were observed with the administration of orlistat in these studies. In a 3-week study of 28 healthy male volunteers, orlistat (120 mg three times a day) did not signiﬁcantly aﬀect the balance of calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, zinc, copper, and iron. Pediatric Patients In a 3-week study of 32 pediatric patients aged 12 years and older with obesity, orlistat (120 mg three times a day) did not signiﬁcantly aﬀect the balance of calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, zinc, or copper. The iron balance was decreased by 64.7 µmole/24 hours and 40.4 µmole/24 hours in orlistat and placebo treatment groups, respectively. Compared to placebo, orlistat lowers BMI with greater fat mass loss than lean mass loss in pediatric patients. Figure 1 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption Systemic exposure to orlistat is minimal. Following oral dosing with 360 mg 14 C-orlistat, plasma radioactivity peaked at approximately 8 hours; plasma concentrations of intact orlistat were near the limits of detection (<5 ng/mL). In therapeutic studies involving monitoring of plasma samples, detection of intact orlistat in plasma was sporadic and concentrations were low (<10 ng/mL or 0.02 µM), without evidence of accumulation, and consistent with minimal absorption. Distribution In vitro orlistat was >99% bound to plasma proteins (lipoproteins and albumin were major binding proteins). Orlistat minimally partitioned into erythrocytes. Elimination Metabolism Based on an oral 14 C-orlistat mass balance study in patients with obesity, two metabolites, M1 (the hydrolyzed ß-lactone ring product of orlistat) and M3 (sequential metabolite after M1’s cleavage of the N-formyl leucine side-chain), accounted for approximately 42% of total radioactivity in plasma. M1 and M3 have an open ß-lactone ring and extremely weak lipase inhibitory activity (1000- and 2500-fold less than orlistat, respectively). In view of this low inhibitory activity and the low plasma levels at the therapeutic dose (average of 26 ng/mL and 108 ng/mL for M1 and M3, respectively, 2 to 4 hours after a dose), these metabolites are considered pharmacologically inconsequential. The primary metabolite M1 had a short half-life (approximately 3 hours) whereas the secondary metabolite M3 eliminated at a slower rate (half-life approximately 13.5 hours). Plasma concentrations of orlistat and its metabolites M1 and M3 were similar in pediatric patients to those found in adults at the same dose level. Excretion Following a single oral dose of 360 mg 14 C-orlistat in subjects with normal weight and with obesity, fecal excretion of the unabsorbed drug was found to be the major route of elimination. Orlistat and its M1 and M3 metabolites were also subject to biliary excretion. Approximately 97% of the administered radioactivity was excreted in feces; 83% of that was found to be unchanged orlistat. The cumulative renal excretion of total radioactivity was <2% of the given dose of 360 mg 14 C-orlistat. The time to reach complete excretion (fecal plus urinary) was 3 to 5 days. The disposition of orlistat appeared to be similar between subjects with normal weight and subjects with obesity. Based on limited data, the half-life of the absorbed orlistat is in the range of 1 to 2 hours. Speciﬁc Populations No pharmacokinetic study was conducted for speciﬁc populations such as geriatric patients, patients of diﬀerent races, and patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Drug Interaction Studies Alcohol In a multiple-dose study in 30 normal-weight subjects, coadministration of orlistat and 40 grams of alcohol (e.g., approximately 3 glasses of wine) did not result in alteration of alcohol pharmacokinetics, orlistat pharmacodynamics (fecal fat excretion), or systemic exposure to orlistat. Amiodarone In a pharmacokinetic study conducted in healthy volunteers who received 120 mg orlistat three times daily for 13 days and a single dose of 120 mg orlistat on the morning of Day 14 co-administered with a single dose of 1,200 mg amiodarone on Day 4, a 23 to 27% reduction in the systemic exposure to amiodarone and desethylamiodarone was observed [see Drug Interactions ( 7 )] . The eﬀect of commencing orlistat treatment in patients on stable amiodarone therapy has not been studied. Cyclosporine In a multiple-dose study, coadministration of 50 mg cyclosporine twice daily with 120 mg orlistat three times daily decreased cyclosporine AUC and C max by 31% and 25%, respectively. In the same study, administration of 50 mg cyclosporine twice daily three hours after the administration of 120 mg orlistat three times daily decreased cyclosporine AUC and C max by 17% and 4%, respectively. Digoxin In 12 normal-weight subjects receiving orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 6 days, orlistat did not alter the pharmacokinetics of a single dose of digoxin. Fat-soluble Vitamin Supplements and Analogues A pharmacokinetic interaction study showed a 30% reduction in beta-carotene supplement absorption when concomitantly administered with orlistat. Orlistat inhibited absorption of a vitamin E acetate supplement by approximately 60%. The eﬀect of orlistat on the absorption of supplemental vitamin D, vitamin A, and nutritionally-derived vitamin K is not known. Glyburide In 12 normal-weight subjects receiving orlistat 80 mg three times a day for 5 days, orlistat did not alter the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics (blood glucose-lowering) of glyburide. Nifedipine (extended-release tablets) In 17 normal-weight subjects receiving orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 6 days, orlistat did not alter the bioavailability of nifedipine (extended-release tablets). Oral Contraceptives In 20 normal-weight female subjects, the treatment of orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 23 days resulted in no changes in the ovulation-suppressing action of oral contraceptives. Phenytoin In 12 normal-weight subjects receiving orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 7 days, orlistat did not alter the pharmacokinetics of a single 300-mg dose of phenytoin. Pravastatin In a 2-way crossover study of 24 normal-weight, mildly hypercholesterolemic patients receiving orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 6 days, orlistat did not aﬀect the pharmacokinetics of pravastatin. Warfarin In 12 normal-weight subjects, administration of orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 16 days did not result in any change in either warfarin pharmacokinetics (both R- and S-enantiomers) or pharmacodynamics (prothrombin time and serum Factor VII). Although undercarboxylated osteocalcin, a marker of vitamin K nutritional status, was unaltered with orlistat administration, vitamin K levels tended to decline in subjects taking orlistat [see Drug Interactions ( 7 )] .

clinical_studies: 14 CLINICAL STUDIES 14.1 Weight Reduction and Long-term Maintenance Trials in Adults with Obesity or Overweight Overview of Clinical Trials in Adults The eﬀects of XENICAL 120 mg administered orally three times a day on weight reduction and long-term maintenance of body weight in conjunction with a reduced calorie diet that provided approximately 30% of calories from fat were assessed in seven multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials of 1- to 2-years duration, and in a 4-year trial. The seven trials included 1,466 patients treated with placebo, 1,913 patients treated with XENICAL 120 mg orally three times a day, and 809 patients treated with unapproved dosages of XENICAL. Patients were 17 to 78 years of age; 80% were female, 91% White, 6% Black or African American, 2% were of Hispanic or Latino ethnicity, and 1% were of other races. Six of the trials enrolled patients without type 2 diabetes mellitus (Trials 1-6) and one of the trials enrolled a population of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (Trial 7). The 4-year trial (Trial 8) included 3,304 patients; age range 30 to 58 years; 55% were female; 99% were White and 1% other races. This trial included a subset of patients with abnormal glucose at baseline. Eﬀect of XENICAL on Body Weight After 1 Year of Treatment A total of 2,680 obese patients were randomly assigned to receive either placebo (n = 1,119) or XENICAL 120 mg orally three times a day (n = 1,561) for at least one year in ﬁve clinical trials. Baseline mean body weight was approximately 100 kg in the pool of Trials 1-5. A total of 1,072 (69%) patients treated with XENICAL and 701 (63%) patients treated with placebo completed 1 year of treatment. information_for_patients: 17 PATIENT COUNSELING INFORMATION Advise the patient to read the FDA-approved patient labeling (Patient Information). Loss of Eﬀect of Certain Medications and Dietary Supplements with Coadministration of XENICAL Advise patients taking cyclosporine, levothyroxine, warfarin, amiodarone, antiepileptic drugs, antiretroviral drugs, certain fat-soluble vitamins, and beta carotene that XENICAL may reduce their eﬀectiveness [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 ) and Drug Interactions ( 7 )] . Liver Injury Inform patients of the risk of liver injury and educate patients on the signs and symptoms of hepatic dysfunction (anorexia, pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, light-colored stools, or right upper quadrant pain). Instruct patients to contact their health care provider if they experience signs or symptoms of hepatic dysfunction [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 )]. Oxalate Nephrolithiasis and Oxalate Nephropathy with Renal Failure Inform patients of the potential risk for oxalate nephrolithiasis and oxalate nephropathy and explain the associated signs and symptoms, including of renal failure. Instruct patients to contact their health care provider if they experience signs or symptoms of oxalate nephrolithiasis or oxalate nephropathy [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )]. Acute Gallbladder Disease Inform patients of the risk of acute gallbladder disease. Instruct patients to contact their health care provider for appropriate clinical follow-up if gallbladder disease is suspected [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.4 )]. Gastrointestinal Events Inform patients of the risk of the commonly-observed gastrointestinal adverse events associated with the use of XENICAL which include oily spotting, ﬂatus with discharge, fecal urgency, fatty/oily stool, oily evacuation, increased defecation, and fecal incontinence. Advise patients to adhere to dietary guidelines to distribute the daily intake of fat over three main meals [see Dosage and Administration ( 2 )] . Advise patients that if XENICAL is taken with any one meal very high in fat, the possibility of gastrointestinal eﬀects increases [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.5 )] .

spl_patient_package_insert: Patient Information XENICAL ® (zen' i-cal) (orlistat) capsules, for oral use Read this Patient Information before you start taking XENICAL and each time you get a refill. There may be new information. This information does not take the place of talking to your healthcare provider about your medical condition or your treatment. What is XENICAL? XENICAL is a prescription medicine used with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity to help adults and children aged 12 years and older with obesity, or some adults with excess weight (overweight) who also have weight-related medical problems to lose weight and keep the weight off. It is not known if XENICAL is safe and effective in children under 12 years old. Do not take XENICAL if you: have ongoing problems absorbing nutrients from food (chronic malabsorption) have a bile flow problem (cholestasis) are allergic to orlistat or any of the ingredients in XENICAL. See the end of this leaflet for a complete list of ingredients in XENICAL Before you take XENICAL, tell your healthcare provider about all of your medical conditions, including if you: have liver problems have kidney problems have problems with your thyroid have eating problems such as anorexia or bulimia have diabetes have a seizure disorder (epilepsy) have an abnormal heart rhythm (arrhythmia) have the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are pregnant or plan to become pregnant are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. It is not known if XENICAL passes into your breast milk. Tell your healthcare provider about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements. XENICAL and other medicines may affect each other causing side effects. XENICAL may affect the way other medicines work, and other medicines may affect the way XENICAL works. Especially tell your healthcare provider if you are taking the following medicines because they may not work as well while you take XENICAL: cyclosporine beta carotene or fat soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) levothyroxine warfarin amiodarone medicines used to treat seizures (antiepileptic). Talk to your healthcare provider right away if your seizures happen more often or get worse while you take XENICAL. antiretroviral medicines Know the medicines you take. Keep a list of your medicines and show it to your healthcare provider and pharmacist when you get a new medicine. How should I take XENICAL? Take XENICAL exactly as your healthcare provider tells you to take it. Your healthcare provider will tell you how much XENICAL to take and when to take it. Take XENICAL with your main meals that have fat in them or up to 1 hour after your meal. If you miss a meal or have a meal that does not have fat in it, you can skip your dose of XENICAL. Take your next dose of XENICAL at your next scheduled main meal that has fat in it. If you take cyclosporine, take XENICAL 3 hours after you take cyclosporine. Take a multivitamin at least 2 hours before or after you take XENICAL, or at bedtime. If you take levothyroxine, take XENICAL and levothyroxine at least 4 hours apart. Spread your daily fat, carbohydrates and protein over three main meals. Take XENICAL with a nutritionally balanced, low-calorie diet that has no more than about 30% of calories from fat (see Table 1 ). Taking XENICAL with any meal high in fat (more than 30% fat) may make the common side effects worse. Table 1. Recommended Daily Grams of Fat Based on Daily Calorie Intake IF YOUR DAILY CALORIE INTAKE IS: THE RECOMMENDED DAILY GRAMS OF FAT (in a 30% fat diet) ARE: 1500 calories - 50 grams fat 1600 calories - 53 grams fat 1800 calories - 60 grams fat 2000 calories - 67 grams fat If you take too much XENICAL, call your healthcare provider or Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222 or go to the nearest hospital emergency room right away. What are the possible side effects of XENICAL? XENICAL may cause serious side effects, including: lowered absorption of certain vitamins and medicines in your body. See How should I take XENICAL? severe liver problems. Stop taking XENICAL and call your healthcare provider right away if you have the following symptoms of liver problems: o loss of appetite o itchy skin o yellowing of your skin or the white part of your eyes o amber-colored urine o light-colored bowel movements (stools) o pain in the upper right portion of your stomach kidney problems. Your healthcare provider may do certain tests to check your kidney function during treatment with XENICAL. Call your healthcare provider right away if you have the following symptoms of kidney problems: o swelling, especially of the legs and feet o little or no urine output o frequent or painful urination o blood in the urine o loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting o severe pain in the back, belly or groin gallbladder problems (gallstones). Call your healthcare provider right away if you have the following symptoms of gallstones: o pain in the upper right portion of your stomach o nausea o vomiting stomach problems. If you take XENICAL with a meal that is too high in fat it may increase your chance of having stomach problems. If you take XENICAL with any one meal that is very high in fat the chances that you will have stomach problems will increase. See the most common side effects of XENICAL. Follow the diet guidelines in the How should I take XENICAL section of this patient information leaflet. The most common side effects of XENICAL include: oily rectal discharge that may be clear or have an orange or brown color passing gas with oily discharge that may be clear or have an orange or brown color urgent need to have a bowel movement oily or fatty stools increased number of bowel movements being unable to control your bowel movements These are not all the possible side effects of XENICAL. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088. How should I store XENICAL? Store XENICAL at room temperature between 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep XENICAL in a tightly closed container. Keep XENICAL and all medicines out of the reach of children. General information about the safe and effective use of XENICAL Medicines are sometimes prescribed for purposes other than those listed in a Patient Information leaflet. Do not use XENICAL for a condition for which it was not prescribed. Do not give XENICAL to other people, even if they have the same symptoms that you have. It may harm them. You can ask your pharmacist or healthcare provider for information about XENICAL that is written for health professionals. For more information, call the Safety Call Center at 1-888-236-5445. What are the ingredients in XENICAL? Active Ingredient: orlistat Inactive Ingredients: microcrystalline cellulose, povidone, sodium lauryl sulfate, sodium starch glycolate, and talc. adverse_reactions: 6 ADVERSE REACTIONS Most common treatment emergent adverse reactions (≥5% and at least twice that of placebo) include oily spotting, flatus with discharge, fecal urgency, fatty/oily stool, oily evacuation, increased defecation and fecal incontinence. ( 6.1 ) To report SUSPECTED ADVERSE REACTIONS, contact the Safety Call Center at 1-888-236-5445 or FDA at 1‑800‑FDA‑1088 (1-800-332-1088) or www.fda.gov/medwatch. 6.1 Clinical Trials Experience Because clinical trials are conducted under widely varying conditions, adverse reaction rates observed in the clinical trials of a drug cannot be directly compared to rates in the clinical trials of another drug and may not reflect the rates observed in patients. Most Commonly Observed Adverse Reactions during 1 Year of Treatment ORLISTAT was evaluated for safety in adults with obesity or overweight with at least one comorbid condition in seven multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials of 1- to 2-years duration, and in a 4-year trial. The seven trials included 1,466 patients treated with placebo, 1,913 patients treated with ORLISTAT 120 mg orally three times a day, and 809 patients treated with unapproved dosages of ORLISTAT. Age of the patients ranged from 17 to 78 years; 80% were female, 91% White, 6% Black or African American, 2% were of Hispanic or Latino ethnicity, and 1% of other races. Six of the trials enrolled patients without type 2 diabetes mellitus (Trials 1-6) and one of the trials enrolled a population of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (Trial 7). The 4-year trial (Trial 8) included 3,304 patients, age range 30-58 years; 55% were female; 99% were White and 1% other races. This trial included a subset of patients with abnormal glucose at baseline [see Clinical Studies ( 14.1 )] . In placebo-controlled clinical trials, 9% of patients treated with ORLISTAT discontinued treatment due to adverse reactions, compared with 5% of placebo-treated patients. use_in_specific_populations: 8 USE IN SPECIFIC POPULATIONS 8.1 Pregnancy Risk Summary Available data from published prospective and retrospective cohort studies over decades of use with ORLISTAT during pregnancy have not identiﬁed an increased risk of major birth defects, miscarriage or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. However, weight loss oﬀers no beneﬁt to a pregnant patient and may result in a small for gestational age infant. When a pregnancy is recognized, advise the pregnant patient of the risk to a fetus and discontinue ORLISTAT ( see Clinical Considerations ). Oral administration of orlistat to pregnant rats and rabbits during the period of organogenesis did not show any adverse embryofetal eﬀects at doses 23 times and 47 times, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on body surface area (mg/m 2 ) ( see Data ). The background risk of major birth defects and miscarriage for the indicated population is unknown. All pregnancies have a background risk of birth defect, loss, or other adverse outcomes. In the U.S. general population, the estimated background risk of major birth defects and miscarriage in clinically recognized pregnancies is 2 to 4% and 15 to 20%, respectively. Clinical Considerations Disease-associated maternal and/or embryo/fetal risk Appropriate weight gain based on pre-pregnancy weight is currently recommended for all pregnant patients, including those who have overweight or obesity, because of the obligatory weight gain that occurs in maternal tissues during pregnancy. Data Animal Data In embryofetal development studies in pregnant rats and rabbits administered orlistat during organogenesis, no adverse embryofetal eﬀects were seen at doses up to 800 mg/kg/day, corresponding to 23 times and 47 times MRHD, respectively based on body surface area (mg/m 2 ). In a pre- and post-natal development study in pregnant rats dosed orlistat during gestation through lactation, no adverse developmental eﬀects were observed in the oﬀspring at doses up to 400 mg/kg/day, corresponding to 12 times MRHD, based on body surface area (mg/m 2 ). 8.2 Lactation Risk Summary There are no data on the presence of ORLISTAT or its metabolite in either human or animal milk, the eﬀects on the breastfed infant, or the eﬀects on milk production. The developmental and health beneﬁts of breastfeeding should be considered along with the mother’s clinical need for ORLISTAT and any potential adverse eﬀects on the breastfed infant from ORLISTAT or from the underlying maternal condition. 8.4 Pediatric Use The safety and eﬀectiveness of ORLISTAT in combination with a reduced calorie diet and increased physical activity to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction long term have been established in pediatric patients aged 12 years and older with obesity. Use of ORLISTAT in this indication is supported by a 54-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 539 pediatric patients aged 12 years and older with obesity (deﬁned as a baseline BMI that was 2 units greater than the US weighted mean for the 95 th percentile based on age and sex) [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 ), Clinical Studies ( 14.2 )] and from trials in adult patients with obesity [see Clinical Studies ( 14.1 )] . Adverse reactions with ORLISTAT treatment in pediatric patients aged 12 years and older were generally similar to those reported in adults [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )] . The safety and eﬀectiveness of ORLISTAT have not been established in pediatric patients less than 12 years of age. 8.5 Geriatric Use Clinical studies of ORLISTAT did not include sufficient numbers of patients aged 65 years and older to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients [see Clinical Studies ( 14.1 )] .

clinical_pharmacology: 12 CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY 12.1 Mechanism of Action Orlistat is a reversible inhibitor of gastrointestinal lipases. It exerts its therapeutic activity in the lumen of the stomach and small intestine by forming a covalent bond with the active serine residue site of gastric and pancreatic lipases. The inactivated enzymes are thus unavailable to hydrolyze dietary fat in the form of triglycerides into absorbable free fatty acids and monoglycerides. Undigested triglycerides are not absorbed, resulting in a caloric deﬁcit. 12.2 Pharmacodynamics Dose-response Relationship The dose-response relationship for orlistat in adult human volunteers is shown in Figure 1. The eﬀect is the percentage of ingested fat excreted, referred to as fecal fat excretion percentage. Both individual data (open circles) and the curve predicted for the population with the maximum-eﬀect model (continuous line) are shown in Figure 1. Figure 1 Dose-Response Relationship for Orlistat in Adult Human Volunteers At the recommended therapeutic dose of 120 mg three times a day, orlistat inhibits dietary fat absorption by approximately 30% in adult patients. Orlistat-treated pediatric patients excreted more fecal fat daily (27% of dietary intake) than placebo-treated pediatric patients (7% of dietary intake). The magnitude of fecal fat excretion was consistent with that in adults (approximately 30%). Ethanol does not aﬀect orlistat’s eﬀect on preventing the absorption of fat. Based on fecal fat measurements, the eﬀect of orlistat is seen as soon as 24 to 48 hours after dosing. Upon discontinuation of therapy, fecal fat content usually returns to pretreatment levels within 48 to 72 hours. Other Short-term Studies Adult Patients In several studies of up to 6-weeks duration, the eﬀects of therapeutic doses of orlistat on gastrointestinal and systemic physiological processes were assessed in subjects with normal weight and with obesity. Postprandial cholecystokinin plasma concentrations were lowered after multiple doses of orlistat in two studies but not signiﬁcantly diﬀerent from placebo in two other experiments. There were no clinically signiﬁcant changes observed in gallbladder motility, bile composition or lithogenicity, or colonic cell proliferation rate, and no clinically signiﬁcant reduction of gastric emptying time or gastric acidity. In addition, no eﬀects on plasma triglyceride levels or systemic lipases were observed with the administration of orlistat in these studies. In a 3-week study of 28 healthy male volunteers, orlistat (120 mg three times a day) did not signiﬁcantly aﬀect the balance of calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, zinc, copper, and iron. Pediatric Patients In a 3-week study of 32 pediatric patients aged 12 years and older with obesity, orlistat (120 mg three times a day) did not signiﬁcantly aﬀect the balance of calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, zinc, or copper. The iron balance was decreased by 64.7 µmole/24 hours and 40.4 µmole/24 hours in orlistat and placebo treatment groups, respectively. Compared to placebo, orlistat lowers BMI with greater fat mass loss than lean mass loss in pediatric patients. Figure 1 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption Systemic exposure to orlistat is minimal. Following oral dosing with 360 mg 14 C-orlistat, plasma radioactivity peaked at approximately 8 hours; plasma concentrations of intact orlistat were near the limits of detection (<5 ng/mL). In therapeutic studies involving monitoring of plasma samples, detection of intact orlistat in plasma was sporadic and concentrations were low (<10 ng/mL or 0.02 µM), without evidence of accumulation, and consistent with minimal absorption. Distribution In vitro orlistat was >99% bound to plasma proteins (lipoproteins and albumin were major binding proteins). Orlistat minimally partitioned into erythrocytes. Elimination Metabolism Based on an oral 14 C-orlistat mass balance study in patients with obesity, two metabolites, M1 (the hydrolyzed ß-lactone ring product of orlistat) and M3 (sequential metabolite after M1’s cleavage of the N-formyl leucine side-chain), accounted for approximately 42% of total radioactivity in plasma. M1 and M3 have an open ß-lactone ring and extremely weak lipase inhibitory activity (1000- and 2500-fold less than orlistat, respectively). In view of this low inhibitory activity and the low plasma levels at the therapeutic dose (average of 26 ng/mL and 108 ng/mL for M1 and M3, respectively, 2 to 4 hours after a dose), these metabolites are considered pharmacologically inconsequential. The primary metabolite M1 had a short half-life (approximately 3 hours) whereas the secondary metabolite M3 eliminated at a slower rate (half-life approximately 13.5 hours). Plasma concentrations of orlistat and its metabolites M1 and M3 were similar in pediatric patients to those found in adults at the same dose level. Excretion Following a single oral dose of 360 mg 14 C-orlistat in subjects with normal weight and with obesity, fecal excretion of the unabsorbed drug was found to be the major route of elimination. Orlistat and its M1 and M3 metabolites were also subject to biliary excretion. Approximately 97% of the administered radioactivity was excreted in feces; 83% of that was found to be unchanged orlistat. The cumulative renal excretion of total radioactivity was <2% of the given dose of 360 mg 14 C-orlistat. The time to reach complete excretion (fecal plus urinary) was 3 to 5 days. The disposition of orlistat appeared to be similar between subjects with normal weight and subjects with obesity. Based on limited data, the half-life of the absorbed orlistat is in the range of 1 to 2 hours. Speciﬁc Populations No pharmacokinetic study was conducted for speciﬁc populations such as geriatric patients, patients of diﬀerent races, and patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Drug Interaction Studies Alcohol In a multiple-dose study in 30 normal-weight subjects, coadministration of orlistat and 40 grams of alcohol (e.g., approximately 3 glasses of wine) did not result in alteration of alcohol pharmacokinetics, orlistat pharmacodynamics (fecal fat excretion), or systemic exposure to orlistat. Amiodarone In a pharmacokinetic study conducted in healthy volunteers who received 120 mg orlistat three times daily for 13 days and a single dose of 120 mg orlistat on the morning of Day 14 co-administered with a single dose of 1,200 mg amiodarone on Day 4, a 23 to 27% reduction in the systemic exposure to amiodarone and desethylamiodarone was observed [see Drug Interactions ( 7 )] . The eﬀect of commencing orlistat treatment in patients on stable amiodarone therapy has not been studied. Cyclosporine In a multiple-dose study, coadministration of 50 mg cyclosporine twice daily with 120 mg orlistat three times daily decreased cyclosporine AUC and C max by 31% and 25%, respectively. In the same study, administration of 50 mg cyclosporine twice daily three hours after the administration of 120 mg orlistat three times daily decreased cyclosporine AUC and C max by 17% and 4%, respectively. Digoxin In 12 normal-weight subjects receiving orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 6 days, orlistat did not alter the pharmacokinetics of a single dose of digoxin. Fat-soluble Vitamin Supplements and Analogues A pharmacokinetic interaction study showed a 30% reduction in beta-carotene supplement absorption when concomitantly administered with orlistat. Orlistat inhibited absorption of a vitamin E acetate supplement by approximately 60%. The eﬀect of orlistat on the absorption of supplemental vitamin D, vitamin A, and nutritionally-derived vitamin K is not known. Glyburide In 12 normal-weight subjects receiving orlistat 80 mg three times a day for 5 days, orlistat did not alter the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics (blood glucose-lowering) of glyburide. Nifedipine (extended-release tablets) In 17 normal-weight subjects receiving orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 6 days, orlistat did not alter the bioavailability of nifedipine (extended-release tablets). Oral Contraceptives In 20 normal-weight female subjects, the treatment of orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 23 days resulted in no changes in the ovulation-suppressing action of oral contraceptives. Phenytoin In 12 normal-weight subjects receiving orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 7 days, orlistat did not alter the pharmacokinetics of a single 300-mg dose of phenytoin. Pravastatin In a 2-way crossover study of 24 normal-weight, mildly hypercholesterolemic patients receiving orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 6 days, orlistat did not aﬀect the pharmacokinetics of pravastatin. Warfarin In 12 normal-weight subjects, administration of orlistat 120 mg three times a day for 16 days did not result in any change in either warfarin pharmacokinetics (both R- and S-enantiomers) or pharmacodynamics (prothrombin time and serum Factor VII). Although undercarboxylated osteocalcin, a marker of vitamin K nutritional status, was unaltered with orlistat administration, vitamin K levels tended to decline in subjects taking orlistat [see Drug Interactions ( 7 )] .

Orlistat was not carcinogenic up to the highest doses tested in rats and mice, representing 46 times and 38 times the maximum recommended human dose, respectively, based on area under concentration vs time curve of total drug-related material. Orlistat had no detectable mutagenic or genotoxic activity as determined by the Ames test, a mammalian forward mutation assay (V79/HPRT), an in vitro clastogenesis assay in peripheral human lymphocytes, an unscheduled DNA synthesis assay (UDS) in rat hepatocytes in culture, and an in vivo mouse micronucleus test. No eﬀects on fertility were observed in male and female rats given orlistat oral doses up to 400 mg/kg/day corresponding to 12 times MRHD, based on body surface area (mg/m 2 ).

information_for_patients: 17 PATIENT COUNSELING INFORMATION Advise the patient to read the FDA-approved patient labeling (Patient Information). Loss of Eﬀect of Certain Medications and Dietary Supplements with Coadministration of ORLISTAT Advise patients taking cyclosporine, levothyroxine, warfarin, amiodarone, antiepileptic drugs, antiretroviral drugs, certain fat-soluble vitamins, and beta carotene that ORLISTAT may reduce their eﬀectiveness [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 ) and Drug Interactions ( 7 )] . Liver Injury Inform patients of the risk of liver injury and educate patients on the signs and symptoms of hepatic dysfunction (anorexia, pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, light-colored stools, or right upper quadrant pain). Instruct patients to contact their health care provider if they experience signs or symptoms of hepatic dysfunction [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 )]. Oxalate Nephrolithiasis and Oxalate Nephropathy with Renal Failure Inform patients of the potential risk for oxalate nephrolithiasis and oxalate nephropathy and explain the associated signs and symptoms, including of renal failure. Instruct patients to contact their health care provider if they experience signs or symptoms of oxalate nephrolithiasis or oxalate nephropathy [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )]. Acute Gallbladder Disease Inform patients of the risk of acute gallbladder disease. Instruct patients to contact their health care provider for appropriate clinical follow-up if gallbladder disease is suspected [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.4 )]. Gastrointestinal Events Inform patients of the risk of the commonly-observed gastrointestinal adverse events associated with the use of ORLISTAT which include oily spotting, ﬂatus with discharge, fecal urgency, fatty/oily stool, oily evacuation, increased defecation, and fecal incontinence. Advise patients to adhere to dietary guidelines to distribute the daily intake of fat over three main meals [see Dosage and Administration ( 2 )] . Advise patients that if ORLISTAT is taken with any one meal very high in fat, the possibility of gastrointestinal eﬀects increases [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.5 )] .

spl_patient_package_insert: Patient Information ORLISTAT (or-lis-tat) capsules, for oral use Read this Patient Information before you start taking ORLISTAT and each time you get a refill. There may be new information. This information does not take the place of talking to your healthcare provider about your medical condition or your treatment. What is ORLISTAT? ORLISTAT is a prescription medicine used with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity to help adults and children aged 12 years and older with obesity, or some adults with excess weight (overweight) who also have weight-related medical problems to lose weight and keep the weight off. It is not known if ORLISTAT is safe and effective in children under 12 years old. Do not take ORLISTAT if you: have ongoing problems absorbing nutrients from food (chronic malabsorption) have a bile flow problem (cholestasis) are allergic to orlistat or any of the ingredients in ORLISTAT. See the end of this leaflet for a complete list of ingredients in ORLISTAT Before you take ORLISTAT, tell your healthcare provider about all of your medical conditions, including if you: have liver problems have kidney problems have problems with your thyroid have eating problems such as anorexia or bulimia have diabetes have a seizure disorder (epilepsy) have an abnormal heart rhythm (arrhythmia) have the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are pregnant or plan to become pregnant are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. It is not known if ORLISTAT passes into your breast milk. Tell your healthcare provider about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements. ORLISTAT and other medicines may affect each other causing side effects. ORLISTAT may affect the way other medicines work, and other medicines may affect the way ORLISTAT works. Especially tell your healthcare provider if you are taking the following medicines because they may not work as well while you take ORLISTAT: cyclosporine beta carotene or fat soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) levothyroxine warfarin amiodarone medicines used to treat seizures (antiepileptic). Talk to your healthcare provider right away if your seizures happen more often or get worse while you take ORLISTAT. antiretroviral medicines Know the medicines you take. Keep a list of your medicines and show it to your healthcare provider and pharmacist when you get a new medicine. How should I take ORLISTAT? Take ORLISTAT exactly as your healthcare provider tells you to take it. Your healthcare provider will tell you how much ORLISTAT to take and when to take it. Take ORLISTAT with your main meals that have fat in them or up to 1 hour after your meal. If you miss a meal or have a meal that does not have fat in it, you can skip your dose of ORLISTAT. Take your next dose of ORLISTAT at your next scheduled main meal that has fat in it. If you take cyclosporine, take ORLISTAT 3 hours after you take cyclosporine. Take a multivitamin at least 2 hours before or after you take ORLISTAT, or at bedtime. If you take levothyroxine, take ORLISTAT and levothyroxine at least 4 hours apart. Spread your daily fat, carbohydrates and protein over three main meals. Take ORLISTAT with a nutritionally balanced, low-calorie diet that has no more than about 30% of calories from fat (see Table 1 ). Taking ORLISTAT with any meal high in fat (more than 30% fat) may make the common side effects worse. Table 1. Recommended Daily Grams of Fat Based on Daily Calorie Intake IF YOUR DAILY CALORIE INTAKE IS: THE RECOMMENDED DAILY GRAMS OF FAT (in a 30% fat diet) ARE: 1500 calories - 50 grams fat 1600 calories - 53 grams fat 1800 calories - 60 grams fat 2000 calories - 67 grams fat If you take too much ORLISTAT, call your healthcare provider or Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222 or go to the nearest hospital emergency room right away. What are the possible side effects of ORLISTAT? ORLISTAT may cause serious side effects, including: lowered absorption of certain vitamins and medicines in your body. See How should I take ORLISTAT? severe liver problems. Stop taking ORLISTAT and call your healthcare provider right away if you have the following symptoms of liver problems: o loss of appetite o itchy skin o yellowing of your skin or the white part of your eyes o amber-colored urine o light-colored bowel movements (stools) o pain in the upper right portion of your stomach kidney problems. Your healthcare provider may do certain tests to check your kidney function during treatment with ORLISTAT. Call your healthcare provider right away if you have the following symptoms of kidney problems: o swelling, especially of the legs and feet o little or no urine output o frequent or painful urination o blood in the urine o loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting o severe pain in the back, belly or groin gallbladder problems (gallstones). Call your healthcare provider right away if you have the following symptoms of gallstones: o pain in the upper right portion of your stomach o nausea o vomiting stomach problems. If you take ORLISTAT with a meal that is too high in fat it may increase your chance of having stomach problems. If you take ORLISTAT with any one meal that is very high in fat the chances that you will have stomach problems will increase. See the most common side effects of ORLISTAT. Follow the diet guidelines in the How should I take ORLISTAT section of this patient information leaflet. The most common side effects of ORLISTAT include: oily rectal discharge that may be clear or have an orange or brown color passing gas with oily discharge that may be clear or have an orange or brown color urgent need to have a bowel movement oily or fatty stools increased number of bowel movements being unable to control your bowel movements These are not all the possible side effects of ORLISTAT. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088. How should I store ORLISTAT? Store ORLISTAT at room temperature between 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep ORLISTAT in a tightly closed container. Keep ORLISTAT and all medicines out of the reach of children. General information about the safe and effective use of ORLISTAT Medicines are sometimes prescribed for purposes other than those listed in a Patient Information leaflet. Do not use ORLISTAT for a condition for which it was not prescribed. Do not give ORLISTAT to other people, even if they have the same symptoms that you have. It may harm them. You can ask your pharmacist or healthcare provider for information about ORLISTAT that is written for health professionals. For more information, call the Safety Call Center at 1-888-236-5445. What are the ingredients in ORLISTAT? Active Ingredient: orlistat Inactive Ingredients: microcrystalline cellulose, povidone, sodium lauryl sulfate, sodium starch glycolate, and talc.
